title: A gate that refuses without a remedy the caller can reach deletes the thing it protects
claim: A validation gate that refuses an action without naming a remedy the refused caller can actually invoke does not merely inconvenience that caller: it silently discards the work, because an agent's response to an unappealable refusal is to route around the tool rather than to argue with it.
expectation: A false positive in a duplicate or validation check costs a round trip: the caller is told no, disagrees, and overrides. The gate being occasionally wrong is a nuisance, not a loss.
reality: The caller does not override, because it cannot see how. A refusal that names no remedy — or names one only reachable by a different caller, such as a CLI flag absent from the tool's schema — ends the attempt. The work goes somewhere unindexed (a scratch file, a runbook, a chat reply) and nothing anywhere records that a refusal happened or that it was wrong, so the gate's false-positive rate stays unmeasured and it survives.
mechanism: An agent treats a tool's refusal as authoritative and moves on; it has no standing to argue and no channel to. So the cost of a false positive is not a retry, it is the whole contribution. The failure is invisible from inside the system because the only trace is in a transcript nobody re-reads.
workaround: Two rules, both cheap. Every refusal names the remedy AND hands back the value that satisfies it — a truncation that fits, the exact override argument, the redacted form. And the remedy must be reachable by the caller being refused: if the tool schema does not expose it, it does not exist. Prefer an override that carries a REASON over a bare force flag, so each use is a labelled instance of the gate being wrong and the false-positive rate becomes countable. Where the costs are asymmetric — a false merge loses knowledge permanently, a false split makes a duplicate that lint already flags — tune the gate toward the recoverable failure.

evidence.command: cairn_record, through an MCP gateway, for a trap distinct from an existing finding
evidence.output:
Already recorded — add an observation to the existing finding instead:
  cairn-0002  ...
  cairn-0004  ...
evidence.note: The near-duplicate gate fires on two shared significant terms in a title. 'an agent does not appear in the panel' and 'an agent does not fire Apex' are different traps that share 'agent' and 'permission'.

evidence.command: the recording agent's own next words
evidence.output: Different symptom, arguably a false merge. I won't fight the tool over it — the corrected runbook already captures the full detail accurately, so the knowledge isn't lost.
evidence.note: It was lost, from the corpus. The agent did not capitulate: recordFinding.ts appended the override hint only when origin === 'human', and `force` appeared nowhere in the gateway's cairn_record schema. It was refused, not told a door existed, and had none.

evidence.command: the same day, a different refusal in the same codebase
evidence.output: Title too long. Trimming. / Still over 120. Shortening hard.
evidence.note: Three round trips because the refusal said 'too long' without saying by how much. Same shape, smaller price — which is what made the expensive one legible.

check.command: D=$(mktemp -d) && cd "$D" && printf 'gate(){ echo "Already recorded."; return 1; }\ngate\n' > g.sh && OUT=$(sh g.sh 2>&1); echo "$OUT"; echo "$OUT" | grep -qiE "instead:|try|pass|--|override|force|to proceed" && exit 1 || exit 0
check.confirmedIf: exit 0: the refusal text names no way to proceed, so a caller that trusts it has nowhere to go
check.refutedIf: exit 1: the refusal names a remedy
check.absentWhen: every refusal in the tool names a remedy the refused caller's own schema exposes

observations.note: Watched live: an agent recording a distinct Agentforce trap was refused as a near-duplicate of two permission-set findings, said it would not fight the tool, and wrote the knowledge into a markdown runbook instead. The corpus lost it and logged nothing. Reading the code, the override existed only behind an origin === 'human' branch and was absent from the tool schema the agent was calling, so 'I won't fight the tool over it' was not a choice. Fixed here by making the override a schema field that carries its reason; the reason is what makes the gate's error rate countable, which it had never been.

environment.note: MCP gateway in front of a production Salesforce connector
